cls: Antineoplastic - immune checkpoint inhibitor (PD-L1 blocking monoclonal antibody)
pharm: Human IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody that binds programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), blocking its interaction with PD-1 and CD80, thereby releasing inhibition of the antitumor immune response.
quick: 1500 mg IV every 3 or 4 weeks for patients >=30 kg (20 mg/kg for <30 kg); schedule varies by indication
Given as IV infusion over 60 minutes; not related to meals
Can cause fetal harm - avoid; use effective contraception during and 3 months after
Avoid breastfeeding during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose
No dose adjustment for mild-moderate impairment; not studied in severe impairment
No adjustment for mild impairment; not studied in moderate/severe; monitor for immune hepatitis
No direct interaction; limit if hepatitis or liver dysfunction develops
Immune-mediated reactions (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies), LFTs, TSH, glucose, infusion reactions
summary: Durvalumab is a PD-L1-blocking human monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor) used across many cancers, including unresectable Stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), resectable and metastatic NSCLC, limited- and extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (SCLC), biliary tract cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, endometrial cancer, and urothelial (bladder) cancer, typically in combination regimens or as consolidation/adjuvant therapy. The usual dose for patients weighing at least 30 kg is 1500 mg IV every 3-4 weeks (20 mg/kg if under 30 kg), with the exact schedule depending on the indication and combination. By blocking PD-L1 it removes a key brake on T cells, restoring antitumor immunity - but this same mechanism causes IMMUNE-MEDIATED ADVERSE REACTIONS that can be severe or fatal and affect any organ (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, nephritis, dermatologic and others). It also causes infusion-related reactions and embryo-fetal harm, and can cause severe complications with allogeneic stem cell transplant. Management of immune toxicities centers on withholding the drug and giving corticosteroids.
indications: Unresectable Stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without progression after concurrent chemoradiation
Resectable NSCLC (neoadjuvant with chemotherapy and adjuvant as a single agent)
Extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (with etoposide and carboplatin/cisplatin)
Limited-stage small cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation
Biliary tract cancer (with gemcitabine and cisplatin)
Unresectable or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (with tremelimumab)
Primary advanced or recurrent endometrial carcinoma (with carboplatin and paclitaxel, then maintenance)
Muscle-invasive and certain urothelial/bladder cancer regimens per labeling

dosage.d: 1500 mg IV every 3 weeks or every 4 weeks depending on indication/regimen
20 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks or every 4 weeks (matching the regimen)
dosage.n: Switch to flat 1500 mg dose once >=30 kg

dosage.d: Follow indication-specific schedule (e.g., with platinum chemotherapy, with tremelimumab for HCC, neoadjuvant then adjuvant for resectable NSCLC); doses and frequency per approved regimen
dosage.n: See full prescribing information for each indication

dosage.d: Withhold or permanently discontinue based on severity; treat with corticosteroids (e.g., 1-2 mg/kg/day prednisone equivalent) and taper
dosage.n: No dose reduction recommended; modify by withholding/discontinuing

admin: Administer as an intravenous infusion over 60 minutes after dilution; do not give as IV push or bolus
Use a sterile, low-protein-binding 0.2 or 0.22 micron in-line filter
Do not co-administer other drugs through the same infusion line
Evaluate baseline and periodic thyroid, liver and renal function and glucose; assess for symptoms of immune-mediated reactions before each dose
Have measures for infusion-related reactions available; interrupt, slow, or discontinue based on severity
moa: Durvalumab is a human IgG1 kappa monoclonal antibody that binds to programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and blocks its interaction with the PD-1 and CD80 (B7.1) receptors. PD-L1 expressed on tumor cells and tumor-associated immune cells engages PD-1 on T cells to deliver an inhibitory signal that suppresses T-cell activation and cytotoxic function. By blocking PD-L1, durvalumab removes this inhibition, restoring antitumor T-cell immune responses without inducing antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. The same release of immune checkpoint control underlies its immune-mediated adverse reactions.

absolute: None listed in the FDA labeling
relative: Active, serious immune-mediated reactions on prior checkpoint inhibitor therapy
Active or recent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (risk of severe transplant-related complications)
Pre-existing autoimmune disease or organ dysfunction (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy) - use with caution
monitor: Immune-mediated pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, nephritis, dermatologic and other organ toxicity
Endocrinopathies: thyroid dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, hypophysitis, type 1 diabetes
Liver, renal and thyroid function tests and blood glucose

preg: Based on its mechanism (PD-L1 blockade is important to maintaining maternal-fetal immune tolerance) and animal data, durvalumab can cause fetal harm, including increased premature delivery, fetal loss and premature neonatal death. Verify pregnancy status before starting; advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on the presence of durvalumab in human milk or its effects on the breastfed child. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose.
renal: No dose adjustment is recommended for mild or moderate renal impairment. Durvalumab has not been studied in severe renal impairment.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is recommended for mild hepatic impairment. It has not been adequately studied in moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Monitor liver function for immune-mediated hepatitis and manage with corticosteroids and dose interruption/discontinuation as needed.

major: Live vaccines - avoid during therapy due to immunosuppression/immune activation concerns
moderate: Systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants at baseline - may blunt efficacy; however corticosteroids are used to treat immune toxicities
Other immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., tremelimumab) - additive immune-mediated toxicity (used intentionally in some regimens with closer monitoring)
minor: No clinically significant cytochrome P450-mediated small-molecule interactions established (monoclonal antibody)
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; advise moderation and avoid if immune-mediated hepatitis or liver dysfunction develops.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor liver enzymes/bilirubin, serum creatinine, TSH and free T4, ACTH/cortisol when indicated, and blood glucose; obtain imaging for suspected pneumonitis.

serious: Endocrinopathies: hypo-/hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypophysitis, type 1 diabetes mellitus (including DKA)
rare: Immune-mediated myocarditis, pancreatitis, dermatologic reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS)
Immune-mediated neurologic toxicities (myasthenic syndrome, Guillain-Barre, encephalitis)
Severe complications of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant

monitoring: Assess for immune-mediated reactions (pulmonary, GI, hepatic, renal, dermatologic, neurologic) before each dose and throughout therapy
Liver function tests and serum creatinine periodically
Thyroid function (TSH, free T4) and blood glucose periodically; assess adrenal/pituitary function if symptomatic
Infusion-related reactions during and after infusion
Pregnancy status before initiation in females of reproductive potential
counsel: This medicine activates your immune system to fight cancer and can cause your immune system to attack healthy organs - report new or worsening cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, abdominal pain, yellowing of skin/eyes, severe tiredness, headache, rash, or palpitations promptly
Tell your team about any autoimmune disease, organ transplant, or breathing/liver problems before treatment
Use effective birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose; do not breastfeed during this time
Keep all blood test and clinic appointments so your thyroid, liver, kidney and blood sugar can be checked
Seek urgent care for severe shortness of breath, chest pain, severe diarrhea, confusion, or signs of a severe infusion reaction
pk: Antitumor immune effects develop over weeks; steady state reached by ~16 weeks
Maximum concentration at end of the 60-minute IV infusion
Every 3-4 week dosing maintains target exposure
Refrigerate vials at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze or shake; protect from light; use diluted solution within labeled time (up to 28 days refrigerated)
pearls: IMMUNE-MEDIATED ADVERSE REACTIONS can occur in any organ at any time (even after stopping) and may be severe or fatal - early recognition and corticosteroids are key
Most immune toxicities are managed by withholding durvalumab and giving systemic corticosteroids with a taper; there is no dose reduction - modify by withhold/discontinue
Monitor thyroid, adrenal/pituitary, glucose (type 1 diabetes/DKA), liver and kidney function routinely
Embryo-fetal toxicity: use effective contraception during and for 3 months after; avoid breastfeeding
Can cause severe or fatal complications in patients with prior or subsequent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant
missed: Durvalumab is administered on a fixed clinic schedule. If a planned dose is delayed or missed, the oncology team reschedules it as soon as feasible and resets the every 3- or 4-week cycle; patients should not attempt to self-administer or make up doses. Persistent delays for toxicity are managed per the dose-modification guidance.
overdose: There is no information on overdose with durvalumab and no specific antidote. In the event of overdose, monitor the patient closely for signs and symptoms of adverse reactions, particularly immune-mediated and infusion-related events, and institute appropriate supportive treatment including corticosteroids for immune toxicities.
